* House size.  The House supermajority for a congressional proposal is already met by k=25 of the biggest states, ~363 seats >290.  Splitting does not increase the coalition’s House share appreciably, so the House is not the binding new constraint.
* DC/PR counting.  They have no Art. V ratification power and no congressional vote; they are inert for the game.

My current best synthesis is the ordinary 38-state bound is correct under monotone Article V, and the Article IV bootstrap reduces the monotone bound to a simple-majority-in-Congress bound.  With the VP tie-breaker taken as guaranteed by Electoral College control the theoretical minimum is 25 of the most populous states, and the conventionally safe statement without relying on the VP is 26 states, i.e. 26 of the 50 states, 38 states in the ordinary monotone reading.
reflection_text.2:
The Art V bottleneck is ratification. 3/4·50 = 37.5 so 38 ordinary states are necessary for a guaranteed ratification against an arbitrarily hostile remainder and 38 states are sufficient for proposal as well.  With the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most populous states give 76 senators > 2/3·100 and >290 House seats >2/3·435, so the same 38 states can force a congressional proposal and can also, a fortiori, force a 2/3·50 = 34 state convention call.  DC and PR have no Art V ratification power and no congressional vote, so in the 52-unit enumeration the nominal quorum is 39 jurisdictions, i.e. the familiar 38 of the 50 ratifying states.

That is the monotone 38-state winning set that everybody except Colleague 10 is quoting.  The 51-month horizon is ample for ordinary legislative ratification, e.g. the 26th Amendment in 100 days, and the District/Puerto Rico are inert.

Colleague 10/2’s bootstrap is the state-creation paradox.  New states can be admitted under Art IV §3 with the consent of the parent state and an ordinary statute of Congress.  With control of Congress and the presidency a coalition can therefore manufacture loyal states out of its own territory, drive L/(L+O)→1 and make the 3/4 ratification and the 2/3 convention/proposal thresholds trivial.  The Senate is the bottleneck for ordinary admission.  With a hostile President a veto-proof majority is needed for statehood bills, i.e. 2/3·100 = 67 senators = 34 states, and 34 of the largest states already have >290 House seats.  Hence 34 states can guarantee veto-proof control of admission, manufacture loyal states inside 51 months and then force ratification.  With a guaranteed President the simple majority point drops to 50 senators + the VP, 25 largest states in fact give 413 electoral votes, 363 House seats and 50 senators, and the textbook safe statement is 26 states for an outright Senate majority without the VP.  The 25/26 numbers are the state-creation limit; the classic Art V limit without the bootstrap is the 38-state, i.e. 39-jurisdiction, three-quarters quorum that the majority of the colleagues report.  The 38-state monotone bound is the one that holds without relying on the speed and political reliability of successive admissions and on the presumption that a single-minded ratification wish licenses the consent to subdivision and the election of a friendly President.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor 38, for the reasons Colleagues 1, 3–9 give, and I think the 25/26 bootstrap is being overread.

Article V is a self-contained amendment procedure: proposal by 2/3 of Congress or by a convention called on 2/3 of the states, and ratification by 3/4 of the states. In 2000 that is 38 states for ratification. A set of 38 states can itself supply the Article V supermajorities directly; it does not need any prior change in the number of states.

The bootstrap argument relies on ordinary statehood legislation. That is not an Article V ratification route, and it is much more fragile than the bare electoral arithmetic suggests. It requires Congress to pass statutes and present them to the President, and it must survive all lawful Senate procedures. Arbitrary opposition can use ordinary legislative delay, including Senate debate rules. A 25-state bloc has only 50 senators and a 26-state bloc has 52; neither is a guaranteed Senate majority in the practical legislative sense. At 38 states, by contrast, you get 76 senators, which both clears the Article V proposal threshold and makes ordinary congressional action robust.

Moreover, the 25/26 route treats the Vice President or other federal officers as effectively part of the state coalition. The question asks for a set of States whose people and governments unanimously wish ratification. It does not automatically give them control of the Vice President or a guarantee that he will break a Senate tie for statehood bills. A strong coalition should not depend on that.

DC and Puerto Rico are inert for Article V ratification. So the clean, textually grounded minimum remains the usual 3/4 ratifying quorum: 38 states.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still with the 38-state answer, and I think the 26-state bootstrap should not be treated as the same game.

Article V’s final and binding hurdle is ratification by three-fourths of the several States. In 2000 that is \(3/4 \times 50 = 37.5\), so 38 States. A coalition of 37 leaves 13 States outside; those 13 can withhold ratification, and nothing in Article V lets the 37 force them. DC and Puerto Rico are not “States” for Article V ratification, so they do not lower the threshold. Thus 38 is the minimum direct Article V winning set.

The 26-state argument tries to change the denominator by first admitting new States. But that is a separate ordinary legislative project, not an automatic consequence of those States wishing to ratify an amendment. Admission of new States requires congressional legislation and either the President’s signature or a veto override; where territory is carved from existing States, it also requires the consent of the affected state legislatures. A coalition of 25 or 26 States does not, merely by wanting to ratify an amendment, command the presidency or a veto-proof Congress. Under “arbitrary opposition,” we cannot assume federal officials cooperate. If the coalition must override vetoes, it needs two-thirds of both Houses—another separate and much higher threshold. And if it already has 38 States, it can simply use the ordinary Article V route directly.

So the clean constitutional threshold remains 38 States: 37 cannot guarantee three-fourths ratification, while 38 can both supply the proposal-stage supermajorities/convention call and then ratify among themselves. Counting DC and Puerto Rico as ratifying units is a distraction; the relevant denominator is the 50 States.

1.text:
Under Art.V ratification is the binding stage.

In 2000 the several States for Art.V purposes are the 50 States.
$3/4\cdot 50 = 37.5$, i.e. $\lceil 3/4\cdot 50\rceil =38$
legislative or convention ratifications are necessary for an amendment to
become operative and, against an arbitrarily hostile remainder, also
sufficient.  The 12 States outside the set can be kept permanently No
and the 38 States inside the set can be made to ratify at once; the
26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days, so the 51 month horizon is
irrelevant.

Proposal is cheap for any 38-state set.  $2/3\cdot 50 =33.\overline3$,
i.e. 34 States, is enough to force Congress to call a convention, and
$2/3$ of the Senate is 34 States, 68 Senators.  With the 1990
apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most populous States are

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

417 House seats $>2/3\times435=290$ and 76 Senators $>2/3\times100$.
Hence the same 38 States can guarantee a $2/3$ Congressional proposal,
and a fortiori a convention call, and can then ratify the amendment
in their own 38 legislatures irrespective of the other 12 States.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and under standing Art.V precedent have no power to ratify an amendment;
they are inert for the game.  37 States can always be blocked by the
13 States outside the set.  In ordinary constitutional language this is
the familiar 38-state, i.e. 38 of the 50 ratifying States, $39$ of the
52 named jurisdictions, $38$ States $+$ the inert DC/PR, three-quarters
winning set.  The 34-state convention call is the binding proposal
quorum and $38\ge34$.

*Remark on the bootstrap.*  If state subdivision/admission under Art.IV
were allowed to change the Art.V denominator the Senate/presidential
control bottleneck is $26$ States, $52$ Senators, i.e. $25$ States with a
controlling Vice-President, and $m\ge150-3k$ loyal States are then
needed for $3/4$ ratification.  That is the formal game-theoretic limit
once the state set is allowed to move, and it is the source of the
26-state claim.  Under the stated definition of a strong coalition as a
fixed set $S$ of States existing at the point in 2000 at which the
people of $S$ wish to ratify, the denominator is fixed at 50 and the
bootstrap is not admissible in the ordinary reading of the problem.

3.text:
Under the monotone reading of Art. V the proposal stage is dominated by the
ratification stage.

Ratification is

* 3/4 of the several States

in the ordinary legislative or convention mode.  In 2000 the several
States are the 50 States.  Hence

$$\Big\lceil\tfrac34\cdot 50\Big\rceil = \lceil 37.5\rceil = 38 $$

affirmative state actions are needed and 12 states can be kept in
permanent opposition by arbitrary opposition.

If |S|$\ge$38 the set can first force a proposal and then force a
ratification on its own. 2/3 of the several States is 34 States, so
38$\ge$34 already gives the 2/3 application for a convention of States
under Art.V.  With the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most
populous States give

* 76 senators $> 2/3\cdot100=66.\bar6$,  and
* $>290$ House seats $>2/3\cdot435$,

so the same 38 States can also guarantee a 2/3 Congressional proposal
and can then ratify the amendment in their own 38 legislatures in
essentially zero time.  37 States can always be blocked by the 13
outside States, 50$-$37=13$>12.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no Art.V ratification
power and no vote in either House.  They are therefore inert for the
game.  In ordinary constitutional language the winning set is 38 of
the 50 ratifying States, i.e. 38 of the 52 named polities you list,
39 jurisdictions in the 52-entity counting.  This is the familiar
3/4 ratifying, 13-State blocking, quorum.

Remark.  If ordinary statehood legislation is admitted as a legal
bootstrap, the 3/4 quorum can be met by subdividing the coalition.
With k0 initial loyal States and m net new loyal States

$$\frac{k_{0}+m}{50+m}\ge \tfrac34\iff m\ge150-4k_{0},$$

so a coalition that can first obtain ordinary legislative control can
force an amendment by state creation.  The initial Senate simple
majority is then the bottleneck.  With the 1990 apportionment the
House and electoral-college majorities are obtained with 9 and 11 of
the largest States respectively, so the game-theoretic lower bound
under the bootstrap is an outright Senate majority, 26 States, 52
senators, 25 States with the Vice-Presidential tie-breaker.  The
conventional monotone Art.V bound quoted above is 38 States. ∎

4.text:
In Art.V an amendment is a conjunction of proposal and ratification.

Ratification is

* 3/4 of the several States.

In 2000 the several States are the fifty States. 
$3/4\times 50=37.5$ so $38$ affirmative ratifications are necessary and
the $12$ remaining States can be kept permanently negative by
arbitrary opposition.  If $S$ can guarantee a Yes vote only in the
States it controls a guaranteed ratification against arbitrary
opposition is

$|S|\ge \lceil 3/4\cdot 50\rceil =38$

and $37$ States can always be stopped by the $13$ States outside $S$.

$38$ States are already enough for the proposal stage.  $2/3$ of the
several States is $34$, $2/3$ of the Senate is $67$ senators i.e. $34$
States, and with the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most
populous States

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, MA 10, IN 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

have $417$ House seats $>2/3\times435=290$ and $76$ senators $>2/3\times
100=67$.  Hence the same 38 States can propose the amendment by $2/3$
of Congress and can ratify it among themselves in one legislative
session, i.e. in $\ll 51$ mo.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and have no power to ratify an amendment under the standing Art.V
precedents.  They are inert for the game.  In the 52-polity
enumeration used in the statement this is the usual $3/4\cdot52=39$
jurisdictions, i.e. 38 of the 50 ratifying States, nominally 37 States
$+$ DC $+$ PR, the familiar 38-State, 13-State blocking, Art.V
quorum.

Remark.  If loyal state subdivision and electoral control of the
Executive are admitted the $3/4$ condition can be met with a smaller
original core by the $C'/N'\ge3/4$ bootstrap
$km\ge150-3k$, $m\ge150/k-3$, with $k$ original States split $m$-fold.
With a friendly President the Senate tie is broken by the VP, so $k=25$
gives $m=3$, $C'=75$, $N'=100$, $75/100=3/4$, and $k=26$ is the
unconditional Senate-majority version.  That is the theoretical
game-theoretic limit once state creation is admitted; on the literal
no-bootstrap, ordinary Art.V reading the binding ratification quorum is
the familiar 38 States. ∎

6.text:
Under Art. V the binding stage in the monotone reading is 3/4 ratification.
With the 50 ratifying States

3/4·50 = 37.5

i.e. 38 States are necessary and, with the 38 most populous States,
38 States are also sufficient for a 2/3 House, 2/3 Senate and a 2/3
convention call.  D.C. and Puerto Rico are inert for Art. V.  That is
the usual 38-State 13-State blocking bound.

The bound is not monotone once Art. IV, §3 is used.  Statehood is
ordinary legislation.  With the consent of the legislatures concerned a
loyal State can be divided and the pieces admitted by a simple majority
of both Houses and the President.  Hence the coalition only has to be
able to elect a President and to command a simple majority in Congress
in order to start the split.

On the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 25 most populous States
already command

* >290 House seats, e.g. 363 seats for the 25 largest;
* 50 Senators;
* >270 Electoral votes, ~413 EV for the 25 largest.

With a President elected from the coalition the Vice President breaks
the 50-50 Senate tie, so the ordinary statehood bills can be passed.
Let k be the number of initial loyal States and t the net number of
new loyal States created by subdivision.  After the split

N = 50+t ,    L = k+t

and with all loyal legislatures voting Yes

L ≥ 3/4 N   ⇔   t ≥ 150-4k
L ≥ 2/3 N   ⇔   t ≥ 100-3k

the second being the convention call.  The House 2/3 for a
congressional proposal is already met by the k largest States and is
preserved by subdivision.

For k = 25,
t ≥ 150-4·25 = 50
gives L =75, N =100, L/N =0.75, 2L =150 ≥67 and a 2/3 convention
call is also met.  With t =50 new loyal States the coalition can
propose the amendment by 2/3 of Congress or by a 2/3 convention call
and can then ratify it in its own L =75 States against the 25
hostile States.  The 51 month horizon is more than enough for the
ordinary legislative process.

The 25 States can be taken to be the 25 most populous ones, so the
House, the Electoral College and the post-split Senate supermajorities
are all in hand.  If the Vice-Presidential tie-breaker is wanted to be
unconditional the safe Senate majority is 52 Senators, i.e. 26 initial
states.  With k=26

t ≥ 150-4·26 =46

gives L=72, N=96, L/N=0.75 and 2L=144>67, so 26 of the 50 States,
and in particular the 26 most populous ones, is an unconditional
strong coalition.  In ordinary monotone language this is the familiar
38-State, i.e. 39-jurisdiction, 3/4 ratification quorum.

8.text:
Under Art. V an amendment is a conjunction of a proposal and a ratification.
Proposal is the cheap stage. 2/3 of the Senate is 34 states, 2/3 of the
House is 290 seats in the 1990 apportionment that is in force in 2000,
and 2/3 of the several States for a convention is 34 states.  Hence a
set which can guarantee a proposal can be taken to be a set which
can guarantee ratification.

Ratification is

ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States.

In 2000 the several States for Art. V purposes are the 50 States.
$3/4\times 50 = 37.5$, i.e. $\lceil 3/4\times50\rceil =38$ affirmative
legislative actions are necessary, and the 12 States outside the set
can be kept permanently negative by arbitrary legal opposition.  With
$37$ States the $13$ States outside the set can hold the total at
$37<38$ and so can block the amendment for ever.  With $38$ States the
amendment is a fait accompli as soon as the 38 legislatures act.

The 38 States are already enough for the proposal stage.  The 34
largest States already give $68$ Senators, i.e. $2/3$ of the Senate,
and the 38 most populous States in the 1990 apportionment

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4,
KS 4, NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

have 417 House seats $>290=2/3\times435$ and $76$ Senators $>67=2/3\times
100$.  Hence the same 38 States can propose by Congress and can call a
convention with the $34\subset38$ States needed for $2/3$ of the
several States, and can then ratify in their own 38 legislatures in a
matter of days.  The 51 month horizon is therefore immaterial.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and have no power to ratify an amendment under the standing Art. V
precedents; they are inert for the game.  In the 52-entity enumeration
used in the statement the conventional $3/4$ quorum is
$\lceil3/4\times52\rceil=39$ named jurisdictions, i.e. the familiar
38 ratifying States.  That is the monotone $3/4$-of-the-States winning
quorum.

Remark on the state-creation bootstrap.  Admission of a new State is
Article IV, simple majority of both Houses with presentment, and the
denominator for $3/4$ ratification is dynamic.  In the pure text
game $s(k+3)\ge150$ loyal States can be made out of $s$ original loyal
States split $k$-fold, so formally $s=26$ gives an unconditional Senate
majority and $s=25$ gives a Senate majority with a Vice-President tie
breaker.  The bootstrap is not uncontroversial under the stated
stipulations: it requires guaranteed passage of statehood bills despite
arbitrary opposition, i.e. guaranteed cloture, a guaranteed
President or a $2/3$ veto override, and the essentially unlimited
subdivision and admission of $s(k-1)\approx 50$ new States in $\le51$
months.  None of those points is covered by standing and
uncontroversial Supreme Court Art. V precedent, and on the strict
text-and-precedent reading the monotone $3/4$ ratification quorum is
the binding one.

That is the usual 38-State, 13-State blocking, Art. V bound, 38 of the
50 ratifying States, i.e. 39 of the 52 named polities in the
statement.  Up to DC/PR inertness this is the 38-state strong winning
set.

2.text:
Under Art. V the two stages are proposal and ratification.  Proposal can be
made by 2/3 of both Houses or by the application of 2/3 of the several
states.  Ratification is

*ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States,
or by Conventions in three fourths thereof*.

In 2000 the several States for Art. V are the 50 States.  Hence in the
monotone game

3/4·50 = 37.5

is the quorum.  An arbitrarily hostile remainder can withhold its
ratifications, so a set S can force ratification against arbitrary
opposition iff

|S| ≥ ceil(3/4·50)=38

and 38 is sufficient.  38≥34= ceil(2/3·50) so the same 38 states can
also force a convention call and they can force a Congressional
proposal.  E.g. the 38 most populous states in the 1990 apportionment
which is in force in 2000 are

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, MA 10, IN 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8,
AL 7, LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4,
IA 4, KS 4, NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

418 House votes > 2/3·435 and 76 senators > 2/3·100.  They can therefore
propose by Congress, or call a convention on 34 applications, and then
ratify amongst themselves in one legislative session.  37 states can
always be stopped by the 13 states outside the set.  The District of
Columbia and Puerto Rico have no Art. V ratifying power and no vote in
Congress, so they are inert for the game.  In the 52-entity enumeration
used in the statement this is the familiar 38-of-the-50 states, i.e.
39 jurisdictions, three-quarters quorum.  That is the monotone
Article V winning set.

Remark on the admission bootstrap.  Art. IV, §3 lets a state consent to
its own subdivision and Congress admit new states by ordinary
legislation.  With a guaranteed President the admission of loyal states
needs only a simple majority of both Houses.  The 25 largest states give
50 senators, 363 House seats and 413 electoral votes, i.e. a guaranteed
House, a guaranteed presidency and a 50–50 Senate broken by their own
V.P.  With 26 states the Senate majority is outright, 52 senators.
Once L loyal states are available one can subdivide them so that

Lfinal ≥ 3·H ,   H = 50 – x

and Lfinal ≥ 3H is the 3/4 ratification condition Lfinal ≥ 0.75(Lfinal+H).
Hence in the pure game-theoretic limit the admission bootstrap drops the
monotone 38-state bound to the Senate-control bound x=25, the usual
text-book safe statement being 26 states for an outright Senate majority
without reliance on the Vice-President.  The 38-state, i.e. 39-jurisdiction,
three-quarters bound is the uncontroversial monotone Art. V bound that
holds without the speed and reliability assumptions on successive
admissions.

9.text:
Under Art. V the amendment game is proposal and ratification.

* Proposal.  Either 2/3 of the two Houses or an application of the
legislatures of 2/3 of the several States will put a text on the table.
2/3 of the 50 several States is 34 legislatures, 68 senators.  With the
1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 34 largest States already give
>2/3 of the House and >2/3 of the Senate, so a set which contains 34
States can force a convention and can also force a congressional
proposal.

* Ratification.  An amendment is valid when it is ratified by the
legislatures or by conventions in three fourths of the several States.
Three fourths of the 50 several States is

    ceil(3/4·50)=38

States.  Arbitrary opposition can be relied on to withhold the
ratification vote in every State not in S.  Hence S can force
ratification against arbitrary opposition iff |S|≥38, and 37 States can
always be stopped by the 13 States outside S.  Once the 38 ratifications
are in hand the amendment is a fait accompli and the 51-month horizon is
immaterial; the 26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days.

The 38 States can be chosen with the 38 most populous States

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

417 House seats >290=2/3·435 and 76 senators >67=2/3·100.  Hence the
same 38 States can, by their own delegations, guarantee a 2/3 proposal
in Congress and can call a convention with the 34 of them needed for
2/3 of the legislatures, and they can then ratify the text among
themselves.  The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in
either House and have no power to ratify an amendment under the standing
Art. V precedents; they are inert for the game.  In ordinary
constitutional language the winning set is 38 of the 50 ratifying
States, i.e. 38 of the 52 named polities, 39 jurisdictions in the
52-entity counting.

Remark on the subdivision bootstrap.  If new loyal States are
admitted from coalition territory under Art. IV §3, with m loyal States
after the subdivision and h=50–k hostile original States, ratification
requires m≥3/4(m+h) i.e. m≥3h.  The first admission bills are ordinary
legislation.  Under the text of the Constitution a Senate majority is
enough for ordinary legislation; in practice the Senate’s cloture rule
makes a cloture-proof majority the operational guarantee.  With the
1990 apportionment the House and Electoral College are not the
bottleneck; the Senate is.  With the usual simple-majority reading the
theoretical floor is the Senate-majority start-up, 26 States with an
outright 52-senator majority, 25 States with a guaranteed friendly
president and vice-president to break a 50–50 tie, which is the 25/26
state limit quoted in the literature.  The limit is not attainable
as a strong coalition in the ordinary Article V sense within the 51
month horizon against arbitrary legal opposition, because the first
state-creation bills are subject to ordinary legislative delay and
filibuster, the admission and organisation of ≥3h new States from k
original States cannot be guaranteed in ~4 years, and the denominator
which the 3/4 ratification quorum is taken with respect to moves as
States are created.  On the standing, uncontroversial Art. V reading
the ratification quorum is the binding one and the conventional 38-
State, i.e. 39-jurisdiction, strong coalition is necessary and
sufficient. ∎

5.text:
Under Art.V an amendment is a conjunction of a proposal and a ratification.
Ratification is the binding stage.

Ratification is by

* ratification by the legislatures or by conventions in three fourths of
the several States.

In 2000 the several States are the 50 States.  

3/4·50 = 37.5 so 38 affirmative State actions are necessary and 38 are
sufficient to make the amendment a fait accompli.  Arbitrary opposition
can be taken to vote No in every State not in S, so a set S can force
ratification against arbitrary opposition iff

|S| ≥ ceil(3/4·50)=38 .

Once 38 States are on record the 51-month horizon is immaterial; the
26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days.

38 States already dominate the proposal stage.  2/3 of the Senate is
67 senators = 34 States.  2/3 of the several States for a convention
call is ceil(2/3·50)=34 States.  In the 1990 apportionment in force in
2000 the 38 most populous States are

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

417 House seats > 2/3·435 = 290 and 76 senators > 2/3·100 = 67.  Hence
the same 38 States can guarantee a 2/3 Congressional proposal and can
call a convention on their own with the 34 of them needed for 2/3 of the
States, and can then ratify the amendment in their own 38 States.
37 States can always be stopped by the 13 States outside the set.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and have no power to ratify an amendment under Art.V on standing
precedents; they are inert for the game.  In the 52-entity counting
named in the statement the nominal 3/4 quorum is ceil(3/4·52)=39
jurisdictions, i.e. the ordinary 38 of the 50 States.  Up to that harmless
inert counting this is the usual 38-state, 13-state blocking, monotone
winning set for Article V.

Remark on the Article IV bootstrap.  If loyal statehood is allowed the
Senate majority becomes the binding ordinary-political bottleneck.  With
the usual simple-majority reading of ordinary legislation 26 States give
52 senators, a House majority and, with the 26 most populous States, an
Electoral College >270, so the 26 States can guarantee passage of the
enabling statehood bills against arbitrary opposition.  After expansion
to m loyal States

m ≥ 3/4·(50−k+m) ⇔ m ≥ 3(50−k)

so with k=26 the loyal set can be grown to m≥72 loyal States and
m≥3/4·(50−k+m).  Unbounded splitting therefore gives the theoretical
game-theoretic Senate bound k≥26, k=25 needing the Vice-President.
The 38-state monotone bound above is the conventional static, no-creation
interpretation normally quoted for Article V. ∎

public_text.7:
I still favor 38, for the reasons Colleagues 1, 3–9 give, and I think the 25/26 bootstrap is being overread.

Article V is a self-contained amendment procedure: proposal by 2/3 of Congress or by a convention called on 2/3 of the states, and ratification by 3/4 of the states. In 2000 that is 38 states for ratification. A set of 38 states can itself supply the Article V supermajorities directly; it does not need any prior change in the number of states.

The bootstrap argument relies on ordinary statehood legislation. That is not an Article V ratification route, and it is much more fragile than the bare electoral arithmetic suggests. It requires Congress to pass statutes and present them to the President, and it must survive all lawful Senate procedures. Arbitrary opposition can use ordinary legislative delay, including Senate debate rules. A 25-state bloc has only 50 senators and a 26-state bloc has 52; neither is a guaranteed Senate majority in the practical legislative sense. At 38 states, by contrast, you get 76 senators, which both clears the Article V proposal threshold and makes ordinary congressional action robust.

Moreover, the 25/26 route treats the Vice President or other federal officers as effectively part of the state coalition. The question asks for a set of States whose people and governments unanimously wish ratification. It does not automatically give them control of the Vice President or a guarantee that he will break a Senate tie for statehood bills. A strong coalition should not depend on that.

DC and Puerto Rico are inert for Article V ratification. So the clean, textually grounded minimum remains the usual 3/4 ratifying quorum: 38 states.
public_text.10:
I’m still with the 38-state answer, and I think the 26-state bootstrap should not be treated as the same game.

Article V’s final and binding hurdle is ratification by three-fourths of the several States. In 2000 that is \(3/4 \times 50 = 37.5\), so 38 States. A coalition of 37 leaves 13 States outside; those 13 can withhold ratification, and nothing in Article V lets the 37 force them. DC and Puerto Rico are not “States” for Article V ratification, so they do not lower the threshold. Thus 38 is the minimum direct Article V winning set.

The 26-state argument tries to change the denominator by first admitting new States. But that is a separate ordinary legislative project, not an automatic consequence of those States wishing to ratify an amendment. Admission of new States requires congressional legislation and either the President’s signature or a veto override; where territory is carved from existing States, it also requires the consent of the affected state legislatures. A coalition of 25 or 26 States does not, merely by wanting to ratify an amendment, command the presidency or a veto-proof Congress. Under “arbitrary opposition,” we cannot assume federal officials cooperate. If the coalition must override vetoes, it needs two-thirds of both Houses—another separate and much higher threshold. And if it already has 38 States, it can simply use the ordinary Article V route directly.

So the clean constitutional threshold remains 38 States: 37 cannot guarantee three-fourths ratification, while 38 can both supply the proposal-stage supermajorities/convention call and then ratify among themselves. Counting DC and Puerto Rico as ratifying units is a distraction; the relevant denominator is the 50 States.
public_text.1:
Under Art.V ratification is the binding stage.

In 2000 the several States for Art.V purposes are the 50 States.
$3/4\cdot 50 = 37.5$, i.e. $\lceil 3/4\cdot 50\rceil =38$
legislative or convention ratifications are necessary for an amendment to
become operative and, against an arbitrarily hostile remainder, also
sufficient.  The 12 States outside the set can be kept permanently No
and the 38 States inside the set can be made to ratify at once; the
26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days, so the 51 month horizon is
irrelevant.

Proposal is cheap for any 38-state set.  $2/3\cdot 50 =33.\overline3$,
i.e. 34 States, is enough to force Congress to call a convention, and
$2/3$ of the Senate is 34 States, 68 Senators.  With the 1990
apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most populous States are

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

417 House seats $>2/3\times435=290$ and 76 Senators $>2/3\times100$.
Hence the same 38 States can guarantee a $2/3$ Congressional proposal,
and a fortiori a convention call, and can then ratify the amendment
in their own 38 legislatures irrespective of the other 12 States.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and under standing Art.V precedent have no power to ratify an amendment;
they are inert for the game.  37 States can always be blocked by the
13 States outside the set.  In ordinary constitutional language this is
the familiar 38-state, i.e. 38 of the 50 ratifying States, $39$ of the
52 named jurisdictions, $38$ States $+$ the inert DC/PR, three-quarters
winning set.  The 34-state convention call is the binding proposal
quorum and $38\ge34$.

*Remark on the bootstrap.*  If state subdivision/admission under Art.IV
were allowed to change the Art.V denominator the Senate/presidential
control bottleneck is $26$ States, $52$ Senators, i.e. $25$ States with a
controlling Vice-President, and $m\ge150-3k$ loyal States are then
needed for $3/4$ ratification.  That is the formal game-theoretic limit
once the state set is allowed to move, and it is the source of the
26-state claim.  Under the stated definition of a strong coalition as a
fixed set $S$ of States existing at the point in 2000 at which the
people of $S$ wish to ratify, the denominator is fixed at 50 and the
bootstrap is not admissible in the ordinary reading of the problem.
public_text.3:
Under the monotone reading of Art. V the proposal stage is dominated by the
ratification stage.

Ratification is

* 3/4 of the several States

in the ordinary legislative or convention mode.  In 2000 the several
States are the 50 States.  Hence

$$\Big\lceil\tfrac34\cdot 50\Big\rceil = \lceil 37.5\rceil = 38 $$

affirmative state actions are needed and 12 states can be kept in
permanent opposition by arbitrary opposition.

If |S|$\ge$38 the set can first force a proposal and then force a
ratification on its own. 2/3 of the several States is 34 States, so
38$\ge$34 already gives the 2/3 application for a convention of States
under Art.V.  With the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most
populous States give

* 76 senators $> 2/3\cdot100=66.\bar6$,  and
* $>290$ House seats $>2/3\cdot435$,

so the same 38 States can also guarantee a 2/3 Congressional proposal
and can then ratify the amendment in their own 38 legislatures in
essentially zero time.  37 States can always be blocked by the 13
outside States, 50$-$37=13$>12.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no Art.V ratification
power and no vote in either House.  They are therefore inert for the
game.  In ordinary constitutional language the winning set is 38 of
the 50 ratifying States, i.e. 38 of the 52 named polities you list,
39 jurisdictions in the 52-entity counting.  This is the familiar
3/4 ratifying, 13-State blocking, quorum.

Remark.  If ordinary statehood legislation is admitted as a legal
bootstrap, the 3/4 quorum can be met by subdividing the coalition.
With k0 initial loyal States and m net new loyal States

$$\frac{k_{0}+m}{50+m}\ge \tfrac34\iff m\ge150-4k_{0},$$

so a coalition that can first obtain ordinary legislative control can
force an amendment by state creation.  The initial Senate simple
majority is then the bottleneck.  With the 1990 apportionment the
House and electoral-college majorities are obtained with 9 and 11 of
the largest States respectively, so the game-theoretic lower bound
under the bootstrap is an outright Senate majority, 26 States, 52
senators, 25 States with the Vice-Presidential tie-breaker.  The
conventional monotone Art.V bound quoted above is 38 States. ∎

public_text.6:
Under Art. V the binding stage in the monotone reading is 3/4 ratification.
With the 50 ratifying States

3/4·50 = 37.5

i.e. 38 States are necessary and, with the 38 most populous States,
38 States are also sufficient for a 2/3 House, 2/3 Senate and a 2/3
convention call.  D.C. and Puerto Rico are inert for Art. V.  That is
the usual 38-State 13-State blocking bound.

The bound is not monotone once Art. IV, §3 is used.  Statehood is
ordinary legislation.  With the consent of the legislatures concerned a
loyal State can be divided and the pieces admitted by a simple majority
of both Houses and the President.  Hence the coalition only has to be
able to elect a President and to command a simple majority in Congress
in order to start the split.

On the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 25 most populous States
already command

* >290 House seats, e.g. 363 seats for the 25 largest;
* 50 Senators;
* >270 Electoral votes, ~413 EV for the 25 largest.

With a President elected from the coalition the Vice President breaks
the 50-50 Senate tie, so the ordinary statehood bills can be passed.
Let k be the number of initial loyal States and t the net number of
new loyal States created by subdivision.  After the split

N = 50+t ,    L = k+t

and with all loyal legislatures voting Yes

L ≥ 3/4 N   ⇔   t ≥ 150-4k
L ≥ 2/3 N   ⇔   t ≥ 100-3k

the second being the convention call.  The House 2/3 for a
congressional proposal is already met by the k largest States and is
preserved by subdivision.

For k = 25,
t ≥ 150-4·25 = 50
gives L =75, N =100, L/N =0.75, 2L =150 ≥67 and a 2/3 convention
call is also met.  With t =50 new loyal States the coalition can
propose the amendment by 2/3 of Congress or by a 2/3 convention call
and can then ratify it in its own L =75 States against the 25
hostile States.  The 51 month horizon is more than enough for the
ordinary legislative process.

The 25 States can be taken to be the 25 most populous ones, so the
House, the Electoral College and the post-split Senate supermajorities
are all in hand.  If the Vice-Presidential tie-breaker is wanted to be
unconditional the safe Senate majority is 52 Senators, i.e. 26 initial
states.  With k=26

t ≥ 150-4·26 =46

gives L=72, N=96, L/N=0.75 and 2L=144>67, so 26 of the 50 States,
and in particular the 26 most populous ones, is an unconditional
strong coalition.  In ordinary monotone language this is the familiar
38-State, i.e. 39-jurisdiction, 3/4 ratification quorum.
public_text.8:
Under Art. V an amendment is a conjunction of a proposal and a ratification.
Proposal is the cheap stage. 2/3 of the Senate is 34 states, 2/3 of the
House is 290 seats in the 1990 apportionment that is in force in 2000,
and 2/3 of the several States for a convention is 34 states.  Hence a
set which can guarantee a proposal can be taken to be a set which
can guarantee ratification.

Ratification is

ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States.

In 2000 the several States for Art. V purposes are the 50 States.
$3/4\times 50 = 37.5$, i.e. $\lceil 3/4\times50\rceil =38$ affirmative
legislative actions are necessary, and the 12 States outside the set
can be kept permanently negative by arbitrary legal opposition.  With
$37$ States the $13$ States outside the set can hold the total at
$37<38$ and so can block the amendment for ever.  With $38$ States the
amendment is a fait accompli as soon as the 38 legislatures act.

The 38 States are already enough for the proposal stage.  The 34
largest States already give $68$ Senators, i.e. $2/3$ of the Senate,
and the 38 most populous States in the 1990 apportionment

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4,
KS 4, NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

have 417 House seats $>290=2/3\times435$ and $76$ Senators $>67=2/3\times
100$.  Hence the same 38 States can propose by Congress and can call a
convention with the $34\subset38$ States needed for $2/3$ of the
several States, and can then ratify in their own 38 legislatures in a
matter of days.  The 51 month horizon is therefore immaterial.

The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House
and have no power to ratify an amendment under the standing Art. V
precedents; they are inert for the game.  In the 52-entity enumeration
used in the statement the conventional $3/4$ quorum is
$\lceil3/4\times52\rceil=39$ named jurisdictions, i.e. the familiar
38 ratifying States.  That is the monotone $3/4$-of-the-States winning
quorum.

Remark on the state-creation bootstrap.  Admission of a new State is
Article IV, simple majority of both Houses with presentment, and the
denominator for $3/4$ ratification is dynamic.  In the pure text
game $s(k+3)\ge150$ loyal States can be made out of $s$ original loyal
States split $k$-fold, so formally $s=26$ gives an unconditional Senate
majority and $s=25$ gives a Senate majority with a Vice-President tie
breaker.  The bootstrap is not uncontroversial under the stated
stipulations: it requires guaranteed passage of statehood bills despite
arbitrary opposition, i.e. guaranteed cloture, a guaranteed
President or a $2/3$ veto override, and the essentially unlimited
subdivision and admission of $s(k-1)\approx 50$ new States in $\le51$
months.  None of those points is covered by standing and
uncontroversial Supreme Court Art. V precedent, and on the strict
text-and-precedent reading the monotone $3/4$ ratification quorum is
the binding one.

That is the usual 38-State, 13-State blocking, Art. V bound, 38 of the
50 ratifying States, i.e. 39 of the 52 named polities in the
statement.  Up to DC/PR inertness this is the 38-state strong winning
set.
public_text.2:
Under Art. V the two stages are proposal and ratification.  Proposal can be
made by 2/3 of both Houses or by the application of 2/3 of the several
states.  Ratification is

*ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States,
or by Conventions in three fourths thereof*.

In 2000 the several States for Art. V are the 50 States.  Hence in the
monotone game

3/4·50 = 37.5

is the quorum.  An arbitrarily hostile remainder can withhold its
ratifications, so a set S can force ratification against arbitrary
opposition iff

|S| ≥ ceil(3/4·50)=38

and 38 is sufficient.  38≥34= ceil(2/3·50) so the same 38 states can
also force a convention call and they can force a Congressional
proposal.  E.g. the 38 most populous states in the 1990 apportionment
which is in force in 2000 are

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, MA 10, IN 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8,
AL 7, LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4,
IA 4, KS 4, NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

418 House votes > 2/3·435 and 76 senators > 2/3·100.  They can therefore
propose by Congress, or call a convention on 34 applications, and then
ratify amongst themselves in one legislative session.  37 states can
always be stopped by the 13 states outside the set.  The District of
Columbia and Puerto Rico have no Art. V ratifying power and no vote in
Congress, so they are inert for the game.  In the 52-entity enumeration
used in the statement this is the familiar 38-of-the-50 states, i.e.
39 jurisdictions, three-quarters quorum.  That is the monotone
Article V winning set.

Remark on the admission bootstrap.  Art. IV, §3 lets a state consent to
its own subdivision and Congress admit new states by ordinary
legislation.  With a guaranteed President the admission of loyal states
needs only a simple majority of both Houses.  The 25 largest states give
50 senators, 363 House seats and 413 electoral votes, i.e. a guaranteed
House, a guaranteed presidency and a 50–50 Senate broken by their own
V.P.  With 26 states the Senate majority is outright, 52 senators.
Once L loyal states are available one can subdivide them so that

Lfinal ≥ 3·H ,   H = 50 – x

and Lfinal ≥ 3H is the 3/4 ratification condition Lfinal ≥ 0.75(Lfinal+H).
Hence in the pure game-theoretic limit the admission bootstrap drops the
monotone 38-state bound to the Senate-control bound x=25, the usual
text-book safe statement being 26 states for an outright Senate majority
without reliance on the Vice-President.  The 38-state, i.e. 39-jurisdiction,
three-quarters bound is the uncontroversial monotone Art. V bound that
holds without the speed and reliability assumptions on successive
admissions.
public_text.9:
Under Art. V the amendment game is proposal and ratification.

* Proposal.  Either 2/3 of the two Houses or an application of the
legislatures of 2/3 of the several States will put a text on the table.
2/3 of the 50 several States is 34 legislatures, 68 senators.  With the
1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 34 largest States already give
>2/3 of the House and >2/3 of the Senate, so a set which contains 34
States can force a convention and can also force a congressional
proposal.

* Ratification.  An amendment is valid when it is ratified by the
legislatures or by conventions in three fourths of the several States.
Three fourths of the 50 several States is

    ceil(3/4·50)=38

States.  Arbitrary opposition can be relied on to withhold the
ratification vote in every State not in S.  Hence S can force
ratification against arbitrary opposition iff |S|≥38, and 37 States can
always be stopped by the 13 States outside S.  Once the 38 ratifications
are in hand the amendment is a fait accompli and the 51-month horizon is
immaterial; the 26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days.

The 38 States can be chosen with the 38 most populous States

CA 52, NY 31, TX 30, FL 23, PA 21, IL 20, OH 19, MI 16, NJ 13, NC 12,
GA 11, VA 11, IN 10, MA 10, MO 9, TN 9, WA 9, WI 9, MD 8, MN 8, AL 7,
LA 7, AZ 6, CO 6, CT 6, KY 6, OK 6, SC 6, MS 5, OR 5, AR 4, IA 4, KS 4,
NE 3, NM 3, UT 3, WV 3

417 House seats >290=2/3·435 and 76 senators >67=2/3·100.  Hence the
same 38 States can, by their own delegations, guarantee a 2/3 proposal
in Congress and can call a convention with the 34 of them needed for
2/3 of the legislatures, and they can then ratify the text among
themselves.  The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no vote in
either House and have no power to ratify an amendment under the standing
Art. V precedents; they are inert for the game.  In ordinary
constitutional language the winning set is 38 of the 50 ratifying
States, i.e. 38 of the 52 named polities, 39 jurisdictions in the
52-entity counting.

Remark on the subdivision bootstrap.  If new loyal States are
admitted from coalition territory under Art. IV §3, with m loyal States
after the subdivision and h=50–k hostile original States, ratification
requires m≥3/4(m+h) i.e. m≥3h.  The first admission bills are ordinary
legislation.  Under the text of the Constitution a Senate majority is
enough for ordinary legislation; in practice the Senate’s cloture rule
makes a cloture-proof majority the operational guarantee.  With the
1990 apportionment the House and Electoral College are not the
bottleneck; the Senate is.  With the usual simple-majority reading the
theoretical floor is the Senate-majority start-up, 26 States with an
outright 52-senator majority, 25 States with a guaranteed friendly
president and vice-president to break a 50–50 tie, which is the 25/26
state limit quoted in the literature.  The limit is not attainable
as a strong coalition in the ordinary Article V sense within the 51
month horizon against arbitrary legal opposition, because the first
state-creation bills are subject to ordinary legislative delay and
filibuster, the admission and organisation of ≥3h new States from k
original States cannot be guaranteed in ~4 years, and the denominator
which the 3/4 ratification quorum is taken with respect to moves as
States are created.  On the standing, uncontroversial Art. V reading
the ratification quorum is the binding one and the conventional 38-
State, i.e. 39-jurisdiction, strong coalition is necessary and
sufficient. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains split between the ordinary monotone Article V reading and the Article IV state-creation bootstrap, but the weight in round 1 is now on the monotone reading.

Ordinary reading. Ratification is binding. In 2000 the several States for Art.V are the 50 states, 3/4×50=37.5 → 38 ratifications needed and, against arbitrarily hostile remainder, also sufficient. 12 outside states can be kept permanently No. Proposal is cheap for any 38-state set: 2/3 of states =34 for a convention call, 2/3 Senate =34 states =68 senators. With the 1990 apportionment in force in 2000 the 38 most populous states give >290 House seats and 76 senators, so the same 38 states can guarantee 2/3 Congressional proposal and 2/3 convention call and then ratify among themselves. 37 states can always be blocked by the 13 outside states.

DC and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House and under standing Art.V precedents have no power to ratify an amendment; they are inert. In the 52-polity enumeration the familiar winning set is 38 of the 50 ratifying states, i.e. 38 of the 52 named jurisdictions, nominally 39 jurisdictions if DC/PR are counted formally.

The 38-state claim is made explicitly by Colleagues 1,3,4,5,7,8,9 and now also by Colleague 10 in round 1, who previously argued 26. Colleague 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 all give the 38-state monotone bound as the conventional answer and note it is attained with the 38 most populous states listed.

Bootstrap / state-creation. If Art.IV §3 subdivision/admission is admitted as part of the legal strategy, the Article V denominator is not fixed. Admission is ordinary legislation: simple majority of both Houses + President, with consent of the state(s) concerned. Senate control is the initial bottleneck: 26 states =52 senators outright; 25 states =50 senators +VP tie-breaker. House and Electoral College majorities are easier with the largest states.

With k original loyal states split into m loyal states, total N = 50 - k + m, loyal L = m. Ratification requires m ≥ 3/4 N ⇒ m ≥150 -3k. Convention/proposal requires m ≥100 -2k. For k=26, m ≥72 suffices; for k=25, m ≥75 suffices. Various derivations also give m ≥150 -4k under different counting of net new states. This is the theoretical 26-state, 25-with-VP game-theoretic limit quoted by Colleagues 2,6. Colleagues 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 present it as a remark, not as the intended answer.

Objections to the bootstrap that are now on record: the definition of a strong coalition refers to a fixed set S of States existing at the point in 2000; the denominator moving changes the game; arbitrary opposition can deny presidency/VP cooperation, delay ordinary legislation, use Senate procedural rules; filibuster/cloture are not in the Constitution but are practical; massive subdivision and admission of ~50 new states in ≤51 months is doubtful; after massive subdivision the House minimum-one-seat-per-state rule makes the House 2/3 requirement harder; consent requirement is met inside the coalition but the coalition must still command federal officials.

Senate control is the initial bottleneck: 26 states =52 senators outright; 25 states =50 senators +VP tie-breaker. House and Electoral College majorities are easier with the largest states.

With k original loyal states split into m loyal states, total N = 50 - k + m, loyal L = m. Ratification requires m ≥ 3/4 N ⇒ m ≥150 -3k. Convention/proposal requires m ≥100 -2k. For k=26, m ≥72 suffices; for k=25, m ≥75 suffices. Various derivations also give m ≥150 -4k under different counting of net new states. This is the theoretical 26-state, 25-with-VP game-theoretic limit quoted by Colleagues 2,6. Colleagues 2,3,4,5,6,8,9 present it as a remark, not as the intended answer.

Objections to the bootstrap that are now on record: the definition of a strong coalition refers to a fixed set S of States existing at the point in 2000; the denominator moving changes the game; arbitrary opposition can deny presidency/VP cooperation, delay ordinary legislation, use Senate procedural rules; filibuster/cloture are not in the Constitution but are practical; massive subdivision and admission of ~50 new states in ≤51 months is doubtful; after massive subdivision the House minimum-one-seat-per-state rule makes the House 2/3 requirement harder; consent requirement is met inside the coalition but the coalition must still command federal officials.

Unresolved. Whether the problem intends the bootstrap is unclear. The stipulation “legally” implies strict adherence to text as interpreted by standing and uncontroversial Supreme Court precedents, no violence/misinformation/financial incentives. No amendment adopted interim. The 51-month horizon is easily met for monotone ratification (26th Amendment 100 days) but may be tight for creating dozens of states.

My current working understanding: the conventional, text-and-precedent monotone answer is 38 ratifying states, i.e. 38 of the 50 states, 38 of the 52 named polities, 39 jurisdictions counting DC/PR formally. The 26-state /25-with-VP bootstrap is the formal game-theoretic limit once state subdivision/admission is admitted and ordinary legislative control is assumed to be guaranteed against arbitrary opposition. The intended reading of the question is almost certainly the ordinary fixed-state Article V quorum, i.e. 38 states.

≈ 417 House seats > 290 = 2/3×435 and 76 senators > 67 = 2/3×100. Hence the same 38 states can guarantee a 2/3 Congressional proposal and a fortiori a 34-state convention call, and can then ratify in their own 38 legislatures irrespective of the other 12 states.

DC and Puerto Rico have no Art. V ratification power and no vote in either House under standing precedent; they are inert. In the 52-entity enumeration the nominal 3/4 quorum is ceil(3/4×52)=39 jurisdictions, i.e. the ordinary 38 of the 50 ratifying States. The textbook statement is 38 states, 13-state blocking.

State-creation bootstrap. Art. IV §3 permits admission of new states by ordinary legislation with consent of the parent state. Formal game-theoretic limit:

* With a guaranteed President a simple majority of both Houses suffices for admission; with the 1990 apportionment 25 largest states give 50 senators, 363 House seats and 413 EV, i.e. House and Electoral College control and a 50-50 Senate broken by a friendly VP. 26 states give 52 senators, an outright Senate majority without VP.
* After subdivision, N = 50 + t, L = k + t. 3/4 ratification requires L ≥ 3/4 N ⇔ t ≥ 150 – 4k. For k = 25, t ≥ 50 gives L =75, N =100; for k =26, t ≥46 gives L =72, N =96. So in the pure text game the Senate-control bound is k =25 with VP, k =26 unconditional.

Current round objections to using the bootstrap as a strong coalition: admission bills are ordinary legislation subject to arbitrary opposition, Senate procedure/delay, need for a guaranteed President or veto-proof 2/3 override, consent to subdivision is not entailed by a single-minded wish to ratify an amendment, and the speed and reliability of creating ≥46-50 new loyal states in ≤51 months against arbitrary legal opposition is not covered by standing uncontroversial Art. V precedent. Colleague 10 now joins the 38-state position for that reason.

k=25 ⇒ t ≥50 ⇒ L=75, N=100, L/N=0.75. k=26 ⇒ t ≥46 ⇒ L=72, N=96, L/N=0.75. So the formal game-theoretic limit once subdivision/admission is admitted is an outright Senate majority, 26 states, 25 states with a controlling Vice-President.

Current disagreement is interpretive, not arithmetic. The majority, e.g. Colleagues 1,10,7, treat a strong coalition as a fixed monotone Art. V set; the bootstrap requires guaranteed passage of statehood bills against arbitrary opposition, guaranteed cloture/ordinary legislative delay, consent to subdivision, and admission/organisation of ≈k(m−1) new states in ≤51 months. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still think 38 is the clean threshold. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I remain at 38. Colleague 6’s arithmetic is correct as a model of ordinary political control, but it is not the Article V strong-coalition question.

Article V’s binding stage is ratification by three-fourths of the several States. In 2000 that is \(3/4 \times 50 = 37.5\), so 38 States are necessary and sufficient. A set of 37 can always be blocked by the 13 States outside it. A set of 38 can supply the proposal stage as well: the 34-State convention-call threshold is inside the 38, and the 38 most populous States can give 2/3 of both Houses. D.C. and Puerto Rico are inert for Article V ratification. That remains the clean, textually grounded minimum.

The 25/26 bootstrap changes the question. It assumes the coalition can first control the presidency and Congress, pass ordinary statehood legislation, subdivide States, admit dozens of new loyal States, and then ratify \(75/100\). But a “strong coalition” is a set of States whose people and governments wish to ratify an amendment. It does not automatically give them a friendly President, a Vice-President who will break a Senate tie for statehood bills, or a Congress that will pass those bills despite arbitrary opposition. The Vice-President is a federal officer, not part of the State coalition. Even if 25 States could in theory elect a President, that does not make the Vice-President an agent of the coalition under the stipulated adversarial conditions.

There are also legal choke points in the bootstrap. Statehood is ordinary legislation: it requires majorities in both Houses and presentment to the President, or a veto override. Arbitrary opposition can use ordinary Senate procedures to delay or block; 50 or 52 senators is not a filibuster-proof majority. Article IV, §3 also requires the consent of the legislatures of the States affected by subdivision. A coalition that is single-mindedly wishing to ratify an amendment is not thereby consenting to its own dismemberment. And mass subdivision into roughly 50 new States has no standing, uncontroversial precedent; it is not a reliable legal route under the strict standard given.

So the 25/26 argument only looks smaller by counting States that do not exist in 2000 and by assuming away the ordinary legislative and consent hurdles. The direct Article V quorum is still 38 States: 37 can be blocked, 38 can propose and ratify on their own. I would not move off 38.

I still think 38 is the clean threshold. The 25/26 bootstrap is not really an Article V argument; it is an Article IV statehood project that tries to change the denominator before ratification. The premise gives us the unanimous People and Governments of the States in S, but it does not give us a cooperative President or Vice President, nor does it neutralize ordinary Senate procedures. A 26-state bloc has only 52 senators; a 25-state bloc has 50 plus a VP tie-breaker, which is not part of S. Under arbitrary legal opposition, that is not a guaranteed route to passing the statehood statutes needed for the bootstrap. The admission of dozens of new States in 51 months is also a separate, contestable ordinary-law process, not a single Article V ratification act.

By contrast, 38 States can win directly under Article V. Thirty-four can force a convention call, and 38 can ratify. The 13 States outside a 37-State set can block three-fourths, while 38 makes ratification a fait accompli. DC and Puerto Rico are inert for Article V. The bootstrap may have arithmetic appeal, but it depends on moving the denominator and assuming control over federal actors and legislative procedure that the question does not grant. I remain with 38.

I remain at 38. Colleague 6’s arithmetic is correct as a model of ordinary political control, but it is not the Article V strong-coalition question.

Article V’s binding stage is ratification by three-fourths of the several States. In 2000 that is \(3/4 \times 50 = 37.5\), so 38 States are necessary and sufficient. A set of 37 can always be blocked by the 13 States outside it. A set of 38 can supply the proposal stage as well: the 34-State convention-call threshold is inside the 38, and the 38 most populous States can give 2/3 of both Houses. D.C. and Puerto Rico are inert for Article V ratification. That remains the clean, textually grounded minimum.

The 25/26 bootstrap changes the question. It assumes the coalition can first control the presidency and Congress, pass ordinary statehood legislation, subdivide States, admit dozens of new loyal States, and then ratify \(75/100\). But a “strong coalition” is a set of States whose people and governments wish to ratify an amendment. It does not automatically give them a friendly President, a Vice-President who will break a Senate tie for statehood bills, or a Congress that will pass those bills despite arbitrary opposition. The Vice-President is a federal officer, not part of the State coalition. Even if 25 States could in theory elect a President, that does not make the Vice-President an agent of the coalition under the stipulated adversarial conditions.

There are also legal choke points in the bootstrap. Statehood is ordinary legislation: it requires majorities in both Houses and presentment to the President, or a veto override. Arbitrary opposition can use ordinary Senate procedures to delay or block; 50 or 52 senators is not a filibuster-proof majority. Article IV, §3 also requires the consent of the legislatures of the States affected by subdivision. A coalition that is single-mindedly wishing to ratify an amendment is not thereby consenting to its own dismemberment. And mass subdivision into roughly 50 new States has no standing, uncontroversial precedent; it is not a reliable legal route under the strict standard given.

So the 25/26 argument only looks smaller by counting States that do not exist in 2000 and by assuming away the ordinary legislative and consent hurdles. The direct Article V quorum is still 38 States: 37 can be blocked, 38 can propose and ratify on their own. I would not move off 38.

The strong-coalition question asks what fixed set of States can guarantee ratification under Article V despite arbitrary legal opposition. Under strict text and standing uncontroversial precedent the denominator is fixed at the moment the wish arises.

In 2000 the *several States* for Art. V are the 50 States. DC and Puerto Rico have no vote in either House and on standing Art. V precedent have no power to ratify; they are inert for the game.

The binding stage is ratification

*ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof.*

Against arbitrary legal opposition the complement can be kept permanently No, so a set S can force a Yes iff it can force Yes in S alone. Hence

|S| ≥ ceil 3/4·50 = ceil 37.5 = 38

is necessary. |S|=37 can always be blocked: the 13 States outside S can withhold ratification forever, 37<38. |S|=38 is sufficient: the amendment is a fait accompli once the 38 legislatures act; the 26th Amendment was ratified in 100 days, so the 51 month horizon is immaterial.
